warmup.q: A Java class needs a handler for ParcelCollected. The Kotlin bus offers fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) and inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>). What can the Java team write?
options: Nothing: Java can't call either function
warmup.why: A Class is not a KClass, so the first call doesn't match, however natural it looks. The reified function is compiled as a synthetic method, and javac ignores synthetic methods, so the second finds nothing. The KClass version works once Java converts the class by hand, which reads badly. This lesson adds a Class<E> overload so Java can write the first line.

opening:
Pedal Post's depot has two doors. Riders who work there every day come in at the front and speak the house shorthand: "PP-7781, collected, two and a half." Drivers from a partner courier use the side door, where a clerk hands them the standard printed form. Both doors lead to the same sorting room, under the same rules.

Our library needs both doors. The Kotlin team wants to wire a dozen handlers in a few lines it can read at a glance. The support team writes Java, and Java sees our Kotlin only through the compiled class files, where a reified function vanishes and a getter is called getWeight-RqKWbHU. The easy trap is to build the side door by loosening the rules, so that Java can pass in raw numbers nobody checks.

A typed event bus gave us delivery. In this last sitting of Part 3, we'll write a small subscription language for Kotlin and keep its nested blocks in their place. Then we'll give Java a door that still checks everything, and finish with a design review. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at a depot with two doors. Now Kotlin callers wire a block with bus.subscriptions { }, and Java callers get a facade that still checks everything.

That's Part 3 in one library. The storeroom's labels became Handler<in E> and the clerk's note, and the cook's note became Rejected. The sign-up sheet became the bus, and the town library's forms and the print shop's units became the model.

Now search your Kotlin code for public reified functions: what does a Java caller see?

Next, we'll start Part 4, Inside the JVM, with a theatre company that fetches each prop only when a scene needs it. Java read our Kotlin as class files. Who loads them, and when does their code first run?

sections.h: A subscription DSL: one block declares the wiring, one handle undoes it
sections.html:
Wiring by hand looks like this: five subscribe calls, five handles to keep, and a lookup in the program's settings between the third and the fourth. If that lookup throws, three handlers are already live, nobody holds their handles, and the program starts half wired. Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers built the fix at the print shop. A DSL, a small language made for one job, is an order form in code: each section is a block in braces, and inside a block you fill in boxes by name. Behind the form sits a builder that collects what the block declares, and an entry function that runs the block and then acts on all of it at once. Inside a block, the builder is the receiver, the object whose functions the block can call without naming it:

Java
// Java, through the Consumer entry point
Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> {
    b.on(ParcelEvent.class, e -> tracking.add(e));
    b.on(ParcelCollected.class, Handlers.timed(c -> loadBoard.add(c), "load", timings));
    b.on(ParcelDelivered.class, Handlers.timed(d -> loadBoard.remove(d), "load", timings));
});
Kotlin
val handle = bus.subscriptions(timings) {
    on<ParcelEvent> { tracking.add(it) }
    timed("load") {
        on<ParcelCollected> { loadBoard.add(it) }
        on<ParcelDelivered> { loadBoard.remove(it) }
    }
}

Each piece of it is a decision. on only adds a Pending(type, handler) to a list, and commit subscribes them all after the block has returned. So a block that throws subscribes nothing, and the caller gets back one Subscription that closes everything, in reverse order, the way nested try-with-resources blocks close. Pending<E> keeps a type and its handler together, so the builder can hold a List<Pending<*>> and still subscribe each entry without a cast. That star is the box whose label wore off, from Star projection: when you don't know the type. We don't know which event type each entry holds, and we don't need to, because each Pending knows its own.

on<ParcelCollected> { ... } is inline with a reified E, so it can pass E::class on: the clerk's note from Type erasure and reified type parameters again. Its body is on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }), and the compiler stops us right there: Cannot inline 'handler: (E) -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'handler: (E) -> Unit'. The lambda is called from inside another object, the Handler, which runs later, long after the function that built it has returned. Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns pictured that as steps sealed in an envelope for the print shop's night shift: nobody may write "stop the whole job" inside, because the clerk has gone home. crossinline is that seal. noinline would compile too, but it keeps a lambda object inside each Handler; crossinline pastes the body into the Handler class the compiler generates.

One mistake the DSL can't catch at compile time is calling on from inside a handler. The handler lambda has no receiver of its own, so the builder is still in scope, and the call compiles. When the program runs, it would add to a builder that has already committed, and that subscription would silently never exist. A check(!committed) in on turns the mistake into an IllegalStateException at the first event, which the bus's try catches and reports.

Before you run the demo, predict the handler count it prints after the block that fails.

code.title: DslDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l03.demo.dsl import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList import java.util.function.Consumer import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.cast // A compact copy of the library: plain ids and grams, a flat-list bus, timing, and the DSL. sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: String } data class ParcelBooked(override val parcelId: String, val grams: Long) : ParcelEvent data class ParcelCollected(override val parcelId: String, val grams: Long) : ParcelEvent data class ParcelDelivered(override val parcelId: String, val grams: Long) : ParcelEvent fun interface Handler<in E : ParcelEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } fun interface Subscription : AutoCloseable { override fun close() } class Bus { private val handlers = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Pair<KClass<*>, Handler<ParcelEvent>>>() fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val entry = type to Handler<ParcelEvent> { handler.handle(type.cast(it)) } handlers += entry return Subscription { handlers -= entry } } fun publish(event: ParcelEvent) = handlers.filter { it.first.isInstance(event) }.forEach { it.second.handle(event) } fun handlerCount() = handlers.size } class Timings { var clock = 0L // virtual time: each read moves it 2 ms val calls = mutableMapOf<String, Int>() val millis = mutableMapOf<String, Long>() fun tick(): Long { clock += 2_000_000; return clock } } fun <E : ParcelEvent> Handler<E>.timed(name: String, t: Timings): Handler<E> = Handler { e -> val start = t.tick() try { handle(e) } finally { t.calls.merge(name, 1) { a, b -> a + b } t.millis.merge(name, (t.tick() - start) / 1_000_000) { a, b -> a + b } } } @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS) annotation class EventsDsl @EventsDsl class SubscriptionsBuilder(private val bus: Bus, private val timings: Timings) { private val pending = mutableListOf<() -> Subscription>() fun <E : ParcelEvent> on(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) { pending += { bus.subscribe(type, handler) } } fun <E : ParcelEvent> on(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>) = on(type.kotlin, handler) inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> on(crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }) fun timed(name: String, block: TimedGroup.() -> Unit) = TimedGroup(name, timings, this).block() fun commit(): Subscription { val handles = pending.map { it() } // subscribe only after the block has finished return Subscription { handles.asReversed().forEach(Subscription::close) } } } @EventsDsl class TimedGroup(private val name: String, private val timings: Timings, private val parent: SubscriptionsBuilder) { fun <E : ParcelEvent> on(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) = parent.on(type, handler.timed(name, timings)) fun <E : ParcelEvent> on(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>) = on(type.kotlin, handler) inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> on(crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }) } /** The Kotlin entry point. */ fun Bus.subscriptions(timings: Timings, block: SubscriptionsBuilder.() -> Unit): Subscription = SubscriptionsBuilder(this, timings).apply(block).commit() /** The Java entry point: a Consumer, so Java lambdas need no return Unit.INSTANCE. */ object JavaDsl { @JvmStatic fun subscriptions(bus: Bus, timings: Timings, block: Consumer<SubscriptionsBuilder>): Subscription = bus.subscriptions(timings) { block.accept(this) } } fun main() { val bus = Bus() val timings = Timings() val handle = bus.subscriptions(timings) { on<ParcelEvent> { println("tracking ${it.parcelId} ${it::class.simpleName}") } timed("load") { on<ParcelCollected> { println("load +${it.grams} g") } on<ParcelDelivered> { println("load -${it.grams} g") } } } bus.publish(ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)) bus.publish(ParcelDelivered("PP-7781", 2_500)) bus.publish(ParcelBooked("PP-7782", 1_200)) println("load: ${timings.calls["load"]} calls, ${timings.millis["load"]} ms; handlers: ${bus.handlerCount()}") handle.close() println("after close: ${bus.handlerCount()} handlers") try { bus.subscriptions(timings) { on<ParcelCollected> { println("never subscribed") } error("missing configuration: load limit") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("block failed (${e.message}); handlers: ${bus.handlerCount()}") } }

alt.title: DslDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.events.l03.demo.dsl; import kotlin.Unit; /** The same wiring as DslDemo.kt, written in Java against the Kotlin DSL in that file. */ public class DslDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Bus bus = new Bus(); Timings timings = new Timings(); Subscription handle = JavaDsl.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { // a Consumer: void lambda b.on(ParcelEvent.class, e -> System.out.println("tracking " + e.getParcelId() + " " + e.getClass().getSimpleName())); b.timed("load", g -> { // a Function1: the price of a g.on(ParcelCollected.class, c -> System.out.println("load +" + c.getGrams() + " g")); // receiver lambda g.on(ParcelDelivered.class, d -> System.out.println("load -" + d.getGrams() + " g")); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); }); bus.publish(new ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)); bus.publish(new ParcelDelivered("PP-7781", 2_500)); bus.publish(new ParcelBooked("PP-7782", 1_200)); System.out.println("load: " + timings.getCalls().get("load") + " calls, " + timings.getMillis().get("load") + " ms; handlers: " + bus.handlerCount()); handle.close(); // close() throws nothing System.out.println("after close: " + bus.handlerCount() + " handlers"); try { JavaDsl.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { b.on(ParcelCollected.class, c -> System.out.println("never subscribed")); throw new IllegalStateException("missing configuration: load limit"); }); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("block failed (" + e.getMessage() + "); handlers: " + bus.handlerCount()); } } }

try.expect: load: 2 calls, 4 ms; handlers: 3, then after close: 0 handlers and block failed (missing configuration: load limit); handlers: 0. With your eager on, the handle has nothing to close, so you get after close: 3 handlers, and the failed block leaves one more behind: handlers: 4. In the Java twin, Unit.INSTANCE appears only inside b.timed(...), which takes a Kotlin receiver lambda; the Consumer entry point needs none.

sections.h: @DslMarker keeps each block inside its own section of the form
sections.html:
Inside timed("load") { ... }, two builders are in scope: the TimedGroup nearest to us, and the SubscriptionsBuilder around it. For a call that names no receiver, Kotlin tries each one in turn, nearest first. TimedGroup has no timed function, so this compiles:

Java
// Java has no implicit receivers: the same mistake must name the outer builder, b
b.timed("load", g -> {
    g.on(ParcelCollected.class, c -> loadBoard.add(c));
    b.timed("deliveries", d -> { d.on(ParcelDelivered.class, e -> loadBoard.remove(e)); return Unit.INSTANCE; });
    return Unit.INSTANCE;
});
Kotlin
timed("load") {
    on<ParcelCollected> { loadBoard.add(it) }
    timed("deliveries") { on<ParcelDelivered> { loadBoard.remove(it) } }   // reaches the OUTER builder
}

You meant "time the deliveries inside the load group". What you got is a sibling group: deliveries are timed under deliveries only, and the load group's numbers silently miss them. The demo prints {load=1, deliveries=1}, where you expected the load group to count two.

The fix is the one that DSL lesson used to keep each section of the form offering only its own boxes. Mark both builder classes with an annotation, a label in the source that tools can read, which is itself annotated @DslMarker, and the nested call stops compiling: 'fun timed(name: String, block: TimedGroup.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. If you really want a sibling group, say so with a label, this@subscriptions.timed("deliveries") { ... }, which nobody types by accident. The marker counts on classes, or on a common superclass, and has no effect on functions.

A nested block that can reach an outer builder will one day do it by accident. Mark the builders.

Java never had this problem. Every Java lambda names its parameter, so reaching the outer builder takes b.timed, and a reviewer can see it. Java pays elsewhere. timed takes a TimedGroup.() -> Unit, which Java sees as a Function1<TimedGroup, Unit>, so each Java block must end with return Unit.INSTANCE. That cost is why the Java entry point, Events.subscriptions, takes a java.util.function.Consumer instead, and why the lab's Java code times a handler with Handlers.timed(...) rather than a group.

In the demo, uncomment the nested timed, run it, then delete @DslMarker and predict the printed map.

sections.h: What Java sees, and a side door that still checks everything
sections.html:
javac, the Java compiler, never reads our Kotlin source. It reads the class files kotlinc wrote, and it reads them very literally. Here is what it finds when Java code meets the API as Kotlin developers usually write it. Every error below comes from the demo:

Kotlin as written What Java gets The fix
inline fun <reified E> subscribe(h) invisible: no suitable method found for subscribe((e)->{ }) a Class<E> overload
fun <E> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, h) callable through JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(X.class) the same overload
a constructor with default arguments new PlainBus() and the full one only: no suitable constructor found for PlainBus(String) @JvmOverloads
a member of an object Registry.INSTANCE.publish(...) @JvmStatic
a companion val SYSTEM Ticker.Companion.getSYSTEM() @JvmField
top-level functions in Timing.kt TimingKt.timed(...) @file:JvmName("Handlers")
a data class with value-class properties ParcelCollected(String,long) has private access in ParcelCollected, getters such as getWeight-RqKWbHU() a facade

Read the table one row at a time with the earlier tracks in mind. A reified function is the clerk's note, and javac can't write one: it can't paste Kotlin code into a Java caller, so kotlinc marks the function synthetic, made by the compiler and hidden from Java source. Type erasure and reified type parameters gave the answer: Java hands over the class itself, ParcelCollected.class, so the bus needs an overload, a second subscribe with the same name that takes Java's Class<E>. The annotations each ask kotlinc for one small thing. @JvmOverloads asks for one Java constructor per default argument. @JvmStatic makes an object's member a real static method. @JvmField exposes a constant as a plain field, and @file:JvmName names the class that holds a file's top-level functions.

The facade is the decision that matters, because it touches the checks. A facade, the hotel reception desk from Adapter and Facade, is one small object that gives outsiders a simple way in. Value classes and what they compile to warned that @JvmName on a function that takes a value class lets Java pass a raw long straight past init. Our facade does the opposite. It takes plain values and builds the value classes itself, so every init block runs:

Java
ParcelCollected c = Events.collected("PP-7781", 2_500);    // validates: "7781" throws
long grams = Events.grams(c);
bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected.class, e -> loadBoard.add(Events.parcelId(e), Events.grams(e)));
Kotlin
object Events {
    @JvmStatic
    fun collected(parcelId: String, grams: Long): ParcelCollected =
        ParcelCollected(ParcelId(parcelId), Weight(grams))          // the init blocks run

    @JvmStatic
    fun grams(event: Handover): Long = event.weight.grams
}

@JvmExposeBoxed, Experimental in Kotlin 2.4 and switched on with an opt-in, would give Java new ParcelCollected(new ParcelId(...), new Weight(...)) and a boxed getter. In a quick test with its module-wide flag, the getter on the event interface itself stayed mangled, so Java code that knows only ParcelEvent would still need Events.parcelId(e). Keep the facade until that changes.

Some of the Java surface came free from earlier decisions. Lesson 2's Handler<in E> shows up as Handler<? super E>, so a Java Handler<ParcelEvent> fits any subscription, and the lab's Java support desk counts failed deliveries with one. kotlinc writes PermittedSubclasses for the sealed model, so a Java switch over a ParcelEvent with one case per leaf compiles with no default. Subscription.close() declares no checked exception, the kind Java forces every caller to catch, so try-with-resources needs no catch. And because handlers and middleware are fun interfaces with void and int methods, no Java lambda ever returns Unit.INSTANCE.

sections.h: Design review: defend each choice, or say when you'd undo it
sections.html:
A design review is a meeting where you explain each choice in a design while someone sceptical asks why. It's where you find out which decisions you can defend. Here are the questions I'd expect about this library, with the answer I'd give. Disagree where your program differs.

"Why value classes, if Java needs a facade?" Keep them. In the Kotlin model, a swapped id and weight don't compile, and an invalid tracking number can't exist. The facade costs one file. If most callers were Java, I'd undo it and use plain records with compact constructors.

"A Weight has no unit." Keep it. The one-field rule made that choice cheap, and the door is the right place for any other unit: a partner's pounds become grams in the parser, once. A unit field inside Weight would cost an object per weight and buy nothing.

"Supertype dispatch will surprise people." Keep it, and write it down. The sealed hierarchy keeps the set of keys small, fixed and testable, and the order is a tested promise. The surprise to warn about is the other side of that promise: a ParcelEvent handler also hears every event type added next year.

"in, adapters, casts: isn't that a lot of machinery?" Keep in: it's what lets one tracking handler serve every subscription, from Kotlin and from Java. The single cast is checked by type.cast and guaranteed by the keys.

"Delivery is synchronous and lives in memory." Keep it for connecting the parts of one program. Undo it for anything that must survive a crash or reach another program, because the bus forgets everything when the program stops. Those events need storage that survives a restart, such as a database table written in the same step as the change, or a message broker. Guava's documentation for its own EventBus lists no way to slow a fast publisher, little control over threads and no exception passing among its reasons to look elsewhere. This bus fixes the last one with an ErrorHandler, and not the first two.

"DropDuplicates remembers every event for ever." Undo it as written. Bound it to a window of recent events, or let the handler keep its own record of the scans it has seen, which also survives a restart.

"The DSL commits after the block. What if commit fails halfway?" Today subscribe can't fail. If it ever can, commit must close what it already opened before it rethrows.

Notice the pattern in the answers. A choice is safe when an earlier lesson's mechanism forces it: in for a consumer, no else on a sealed when, a Class<E> overload because Java can't call a reified function. It's a judgment call when it trades cost for safety: value classes with a facade, synchronous delivery, a memory with no limit. Those are the ones to write down, with the condition that would make you undo them.

try.title: Write your own review notes
steps: Without looking back, list five design choices in the library you built across the three labs.
For each, write one line: keep or undo, the earlier lesson whose mechanism decides it, and the condition that would change your answer.
Pick the choice you're least sure about and write the test that would tell you that you were wrong.
try.expect: A strong list mixes forced choices (no else on the sealed when, Handler<in E>, a Class<E> overload because Java can't call reified functions) with judgment calls (value classes plus a facade, synchronous delivery in memory, an unbounded DropDuplicates). The forced ones cite a mechanism. The judgment calls cite a condition, such as "undo when most callers are Java" or "undo when an event must survive a restart".

compare.title: The same wiring from Kotlin and from Java

java.title: LoadBoardWiring.java
java.html: EventBus bus = new EventBus(List.of(new DropDuplicates())); // @JvmOverloads Timings timings = new Timings(); Handler<ParcelEvent> tracking = e -> trackingPage.add(Events.parcelId(e)); Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { // a Consumer: no Unit.INSTANCE b.on(ParcelEvent.class, tracking); b.on(ParcelCollected.class, Handlers.timed(c -> loadBoard.add(Events.parcelId(c), Events.grams(c)), "load", timings)); b.on(ParcelDelivered.class, Handlers.timed(d -> loadBoard.remove(Events.parcelId(d), Events.grams(d)), "load", timings)); }); bus.publish(Events.collected("PP-7781", 2_500)); // validated by the value classes handle.close(); // close() throws nothing

kotlin.title: LoadBoardWiring.kt
kotlin.html: val bus = EventBus(listOf(DropDuplicates())) val timings = Timings() val tracking = Handler<ParcelEvent> { trackingPage += it.parcelId.value } val handle = bus.subscriptions(timings) { on(ParcelEvent::class, tracking) timed("load") { on<ParcelCollected> { loadBoard.add(it.parcelId, it.weight) } on<ParcelDelivered> { loadBoard.remove(it.parcelId, it.weight) } } } bus.publish(ParcelCollected(ParcelId("PP-7781"), Weight(2_500))) handle.close()

compare.note: Both wire the same three subscriptions on the same bus, and both get one handle back. The Kotlin version reads the domain types directly (it.parcelId, it.weight) and uses on<E> with a reified type, inside a timed group whose handlers can't reach the outer builder by accident. The Java version passes Class tokens, gets plain String and long through the Events facade, and times handlers one by one with Handlers.timed, because a Kotlin receiver lambda would cost it a return Unit.INSTANCE. What doesn't differ is the safety: the same init blocks check events built from Java, Handler<? super E> lets the Java tracking handler fit any subscription, and javac can switch exhaustively over the Kotlin sealed model.

worked.title: Add subscribeOnce, with its Kotlin sugar and its Java door

steps.say: A welcome text must go out for a new sender's first collection only. Start with the core, in Kotlin, taking a KClass. The handle closes itself, and compareAndSet makes sure only one of eight publishing threads runs the handler, the balking idea from Concurrency patterns that tie it all together. One race needs care: an event can arrive before handle.set has run, so the code closes again after setting it.
steps.code: fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribeOnce(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val fired = AtomicBoolean() val handle = AtomicReference<Subscription>() handle.set(subscribe(type) { event -> if (fired.compareAndSet(false, true)) { // 1. only the first event wins try { handler.handle(event) } // 2. do the work finally { handle.get()?.close() } // 3. stop further deliveries } }) if (fired.get()) handle.get().close() // an event won before the handle was set return handle.get() }

alt.html: // What Java sees for the core: a KClass parameter it can only reach the long way round. bus.subscribeOnce(JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(ParcelCollected.class), c -> sendWelcome(c));

steps.say: Add the Kotlin sugar: a one-line reified wrapper. It needs no noinline or crossinline: its parameter is a Handler, not a function type, so there is nothing to inline.
steps.code: inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribeOnce(handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribeOnce(E::class, handler) bus.subscribeOnce<ParcelCollected> { sendWelcome(it) }

alt.html: // Java can't see the reified wrapper: javac reports "no suitable method found for subscribeOnce" bus.subscribeOnce(c -> sendWelcome(c));

steps.say: Add the Java door: a Class<E> overload that converts and delegates. Because Handler is declared in, Java sees Handler<? super E>, so a general handler fits too.
steps.code: fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribeOnce(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribeOnce(type.kotlin, handler)

alt.html: bus.subscribeOnce(ParcelCollected.class, c -> sendWelcome(Events.parcelId(c)));

steps.say: Last, pin it from both sides. A Kotlin test publishes the same collection from eight threads and checks that one text went out. A Java test makes the Java call above, so a Kotlin-side change that breaks Java callers fails in this module's own build.
steps.code: val sent = AtomicInteger() bus.subscribeOnce<ParcelCollected> { sent.incrementAndGet() } collide(8) { bus.publish(collection) } assertThat(sent.get()).isEqualTo(1)

alt.html: AtomicInteger sent = new AtomicInteger(); bus.subscribeOnce(ParcelCollected.class, c -> sent.incrementAndGet()); bus.publish(Events.collected("PP-7781", 2_500)); bus.publish(Events.collected("PP-7781", 2_500)); assertThat(sent.get()).isEqualTo(1);

drill.title: The DSL skeleton and the Java door from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. From memory, write the Kotlin entry function subscriptions, the builder's on(type, handler), commit() and the reified on<E> (with the right modifier). Then, below it, write the Java call that wires one delivery handler through Events.subscriptions, and name the annotation or overload behind each part of that Java line.

answer.html: @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS) annotation class EventsDsl @EventsDsl class SubscriptionsBuilder private constructor(private val bus: EventBus) { private val pending = mutableListOf<Pending<*>>() fun <E : ParcelEvent> on(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) { pending += Pending(type, handler) } fun <E : ParcelEvent> on(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>) = on(type.kotlin, handler) inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> on(crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }) private fun commit(): Subscription { val handles = pending.map { it.subscribeTo(bus) } return Subscription { handles.asReversed().forEach(Subscription::close) } } private class Pending<E : ParcelEvent>(val type: KClass<E>, val handler: Handler<E>) { fun subscribeTo(bus: EventBus) = bus.subscribe(type, handler) } companion object { fun build(bus: EventBus, block: SubscriptionsBuilder.() -> Unit) = SubscriptionsBuilder(bus).apply(block).commit() } } fun EventBus.subscriptions(block: SubscriptionsBuilder.() -> Unit): Subscription = SubscriptionsBuilder.build(this, block)

alt.html: Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, b -> // @JvmStatic + a Consumer parameter b.on(ParcelDelivered.class, // the Class<E> overload d -> delivered.add(Events.grams(d)))); // the facade over Weight; Handler<? super E> handle.close(); // Subscription.close() throws nothing

recap: A subscription DSL collects what the block declares and subscribes it all at the end: a block that throws subscribes nothing, and one handle closes everything, in reverse order.
on<E> is inline and reified. Its lambda is called from inside a Handler object, so it must be crossinline. A check in on catches subscriptions made from inside a handler, which @DslMarker can't see.
@DslMarker on the builder classes makes only the nearest builder implicit, so timed inside timed stops compiling instead of quietly creating a sibling group.

Java can't call reified functions and stumbles over KClass, defaults, objects, companions and value classes. Add Class<E> overloads, @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic, @JvmField, @file:JvmName, and a facade that builds the value classes so every check still runs.
In a design review, a choice that an earlier mechanism forces is easy to defend. Write down the judgment calls, and the condition that would make you undo each one.
Where the library stops: it lives in one program's memory, so events that must survive a crash or reach another program need storage of their own, and a slow handler still slows every publish.

explain.prompt: A sceptical reviewer says: "This is a lot of type machinery for an event bus. Why not a Map<String, MutableList<(Any) -> Unit>> and a JSON string per event?" Defend your design: name the bugs each choice prevents, and the one or two choices you'd undo.
explain.answer: With strings and Any, every handler parses and casts for itself: a scan that says "2.5" grams throws inside the load board after the tracking page listed it, a typo in an event name never matches, and a new event type is ignored everywhere without a word. The sealed model and the door stop all three: bad input is rejected once, and a when without else breaks the build wherever a new type needs handling. Value classes make a swapped id and weight a compile error. The bus walks supertypes, so one tracking handler sees every event, and Handler<in E> lets that handler fit any subscription, from Kotlin and from Java. Isolation, handles and a copy-on-write list keep one bad or self-removing handler from hurting the rest. The DSL commits a block all at once, and @DslMarker keeps nested blocks from reaching the wrong builder. For Java, the overloads and the facade make it read like a Java library without skipping a check. What I'd undo: the unbounded DropDuplicates, which should become a bounded window or a record kept by the handler. And anything that must survive a crash goes to storage that outlives the program, not to this bus.

deeper.html:
A production version of this library would add, roughly in this order:

  • Asynchronous lanes. An executor per group of handlers, with one single-threaded lane per tracking number so the events for one parcel keep their order, and a bounded queue in front of each lane. That's also where backpressure lives, the idea of a slow receiver slowing a fast sender: when a lane is full, the publisher waits, or the event is kept to try again later.
  • Real metrics. Replace Timings with timers from a metrics library such as Micrometer, named after each subscription, so a slow handler shows up on the same dashboards as the rest of the program.
  • Durability. Events that must survive a crash, or reach other programs, go into a database table in the same transaction as the change that caused them (a pattern often called an outbox), and a separate job sends them on to a message broker. The in-process bus stays for connecting the parts of one program.
  • A shelf for refused scans. Parsed.Rejected goes to a store with its reason, a counter, and a small tool to replay the scans once the bug behind them is fixed.
  • Versioned events. Stable type names with @SerialName if you serialize with kotlinx.serialization, and parser branches that map old names to new types.
  • A checked public API. on<E> and subscribe<E> are public inline functions, so their bodies are compiled into every caller, and the @JvmOverloads overloads are part of what Java callers link against. A binary-compatibility check in the build catches a change that would break callers compiled against the previous version.
  • @JvmExposeBoxed, once it is stable, if it also covers interface members. Until then, the Events facade is the Java door.

One thing it should not add is registration by scanning for annotations, Guava style (@Subscribe on methods, found through reflection). Guava's own documentation lists the costs: subscribers are hard to find from the publisher, and reflection breaks under the tools that shrink and rename code for release. Explicit on<E> calls keep every subscription visible in the code that owns it.
